analysis.one_liner: Strips legal immunity from big social media platforms when their algorithms amplify content tied to civil-rights violations or terrorism.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 37 cosponsors, all Democrats, but the House Energy and Commerce Committee never scheduled a hearing or a vote, and it died in subcommittee when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a 1996 law called Section 230, social media sites generally cannot be sued over what their users post. This bill would take away that shield for the biggest platforms — those with more than 10 million monthly users — when an algorithm ranks, promotes, or amplifies content that is directly relevant to a civil-rights lawsuit or an international terrorism lawsuit. Simple, transparent sorting (chronological feeds, alphabetical lists, view counts) and search results would still be protected, and small sites and internet infrastructure companies would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: People harmed by algorithmically amplified content: targets of coordinated harassment or civil-rights conspiracies, and families suing after attacks, who today cannot hold a platform accountable when its recommendation system pushed the content at people.

how_it_helps.text: Lets civil-rights lawsuits (under 42 U.S.C. 1985 and 1986) and international terrorism lawsuits (under 18 U.S.C. 2333) proceed against platforms whose algorithms amplified the content at issue, instead of being dismissed under Section 230.
Applies only to platforms with more than 10 million monthly users, so small sites and niche communities are not exposed to these suits.
Leaves ordinary, transparent ways of organizing content — chronological feeds, ratings, view counts, and search results — fully protected, so the target is opaque recommendation systems specifically.

analysis.who_pays: The largest social media companies, which would face lawsuits they currently get dismissed, and would bear the cost of defending them and possibly changing their recommendation systems.

drawbacks.text: More lawsuits could push platforms to remove or bury lawful political speech and debate rather than risk being sued over anything an algorithm surfaced — the classic speech-chilling concern critics raise with weakening Section 230.

The line between a protected 'transparent' ranking and an exposed 'amplification' can be hard to draw, and even transparent view-based feeds can spread harmful content, so the bill may miss much of the problem it aims at.
Civil-rights claims under 42 U.S.C. 1985 cover a wide range of conduct, so platforms could face a wave of litigation whose costs fall hardest on their ability to host open discussion generally.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give victims of targeted, algorithmically spread harm a real remedy they lack today, while carving out small sites, infrastructure providers, and transparent sorting so the burden lands on the biggest platforms. The main honest cost is that platforms facing lawsuits tend to over-remove lawful speech, which could narrow open online debate. On balance it is a focused attempt at a genuine grievance, though its drafting leaves real boundary problems.

outcome.mechanism: The House Energy and Commerce Committee never scheduled a hearing or a vote, so the bill sat in its Communications and Technology Subcommittee until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Malinowski introduced the bill on March 23, 2021, with nine original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology, and no further action was ever taken on it for the rest of the two-year Congress.
Thirty-seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

The bill would amend Section 230 of the Communications Act so that platforms with more than 10 million monthly users lose their liability shield for claims involving algorithmic amplification of content relevant to civil-rights or international terrorism claims.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest social media companies, which kept the Section 230 legal shield the bill would have removed, and people harmed by algorithmically amplified content gained nothing.

for.name: Tom Malinowski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 37 cosponsors for it.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never brought the bill up in committee, leaving it to die in subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican ever signed on, so the bill was a one-party effort that died in a committee run by the same party.

industries.note: By the bill's death, platforms above 10 million users keep the Section 230 shield against suits over algorithmically amplified content, avoiding both litigation and pressure to change their recommendation systems. That shield is exactly what blocked victims of harassment, conspiracy campaigns, and attack-related radicalization from reaching a court.
The bill explicitly exempts services with 10 million or fewer monthly users, and it died, so small platforms were never exposed to the new liability in any case.

industries.industry: Internet infrastructure providers (hosting, CDNs, cloud storage)
industries.note: The bill would have exempted web hosts, domain registrars, content delivery networks, caching, data storage, and cybersecurity providers, and its death left them untouched.
